articles.standfirst: Candidato ao governo do Rio Grande do Sul pelo PCO cumpriu compromissos de campanha no Centro Histórico de Porto Alegre.
articles.summary: Candidato ao governo do Rio Grande do Sul pelo PCO cumpriu compromissos de campanha no Centro Histórico de Porto Alegre.
articles.body:
Candidato ao governo do Rio Grande do Sul pelo PCO, Cesar Pontes cumpriu compromissos de campanha nesta quinta-feira (10). Ele cumpriu agenda em Porto Alegre .

O historiador se reuniu com apoiadores no Diretório Municipal do partido, no Centro Histórico. O candidato debateu o momento da campanha e as estratégias a serem adotadas nas próximas semanas. Ele defende maior participação direta de cidadãos na política.

Até o dia 2 de outubro, os candidatos ao governo do Rio Grande do Sul vão responder perguntas feitas diretamente por eleitores entrevistados pela RBS TV. Serão seis temas, um a cada semana: segurança, saúde, educação, infraestrutura, economia e prevenção a desastres climáticos . Ao todo, 86 eleitores terão suas dúvidas respondidas .

Os candidatos terão 30 segundos para apresentar suas respostas. Dos sete candidatos, três responderão em cada dia . A ordem de aparição leva em conta a mais recente pesquisa eleitoral contratada pelo Grupo RBS , divulgada nesta segunda-feira (24).

Sobre educação , o candidato escolheu a pergunta do eleitor Diego Moura de Oliveira, de Santa Maria, na região Central do estado. "Qual a sua proposta para os professores, para a valorização dos professores, que todos sabemos que é uma categoria que necessita de uma atenção mais especial?" , questiona.

"A educação é um serviço essencial que não deve ser transformado em negócio que vise obter lucro. Nós entendemos que a educação deve ser pública e gratuita e esteja sob o controle da comunidade escolar, ou seja, pais, alunos, professores e funcionários. Nós somos o PCO", afirmou Pontes.

articles.title: 25 Years of 9/11: From personal grief to global consequences, the stories cinema told
articles.summary: Trending News: It seems strange but half the population of the world today won’t be able to answer the question, unlike a lot of us: Where were you when the planes h.
articles.body: It seems strange but half the population of the world today won’t be able to answer the question, unlike a lot of us: Where were you when the planes hit the Twin Towers? The ones who won’t be able to answer the question were either just born or weren’t born the day terror came from the skies in America; and changed the world forever.Twenty-five years after September 11, 2001, the images are still unbearably familiar. The planes, the towers, the smoke, the people running through the streets of Manhattan, the desperate phone calls, the photographs of the missing and the stunned faces of those watching television screens as an ordinary Tuesday morning turned into history.Yet for a generation born after 9/11, these are not memories but historical images. As the attacks recede further into history, cinema has become one of the ways through which the emotional and political meaning of that day is passed from one generation to another.Hollywood was initially hesitant to confront 9/11 directly. The wounds were too fresh, the politics too raw and the danger of turning catastrophe into entertainment too obvious. When films finally began to address it, they approached the event from radically different directions.United 93 tried to reconstruct the terrifying immediacy of the day without conventional Hollywood heroics. World Trade Center concentrated on survival and the extraordinary resilience of ordinary people. Reign Over Me moved away from the spectacle of the attacks altogether, asking what happens to an individual years after unimaginable loss. Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close explored the event through the eyes of a child trying to make sense of a father's death.But the cinematic story of 9/11 did not remain confined to the towers. The attacks transformed American foreign policy, produced the “war on terror”, altered the experience of Muslim and South Asian communities in the West and created a vast machinery of surveillance, interrogation and military intervention. Films such as The Reluctant Fundamentalist, Zero Dark Thirty and The Report examine not only what happened on September 11 but what the United States became after 9/11. One is concerned with alienation and identity, another with vengeance and the hunt for Osama bin Laden, and the third with the moral and institutional consequences of torture.Then came Worth, perhaps the most revealing film in this group because it asks a deceptively simple question: how do you put a financial value on a human life? Its answer exposes the impossible collision between soulless bureaucracy and human grief.Television offered an even broader canvas. The Looming Tower looked backwards rather than forwards, reconstructing the years before 9/11 and the intelligence failures that allowed warning signs to be missed. Together, these films created a conventional cinematic record.Here’s why these fictional stories are a must-watch – especially for a generation that learnt about the world-changing event in classrooms.United 93, Director: Paul Greengrass, 2006Greengrass’ United 93 remains one of the most uncompromising films ever made about 9/11. This film does not reconstruct the attacks through the eyes of presidents, generals or intelligence officials. The director confines much of the film to the claustrophobic interior of United Airlines Flight 93 and the fragmented communications centres on the ground. The effect is deliberately documentary-like. There is little conventional character development, little melodrama and almost no attempt to manufacture a Hollywood hero.That restraint is the film's greatest strength. The passengers are initially strangers occupying a confined space, ordinary people who suddenly realise that the rules governing their lives have disappeared. They have incomplete information, conflicting reports and almost no certainty about what is happening. Their gradual understanding of the situation becomes the film's central dramatic device.The extraordinary thing about United 93 is when facing certain death, courage becomes a collective decision. The passengers are frightened people who understand that doing nothing means surrendering control. Greengrass turns that realization into a study of human behaviour under extreme pressure.The film also changed the grammar of the 9/11 movies to come. There are no reassuring explanations. There is no larger political context given for “better understanding”. The audience experience confusion because confusion was the reality of that morning. The result is uncomfortable because it refuses the emotional distance normally provided by cinema.The film was praised for being rigorously constructed while also provoking discomfort because of the intensity of its recreation. That tension remains important 20 years later.World Trade Center, Director: Oliver Stone, 2006If United 93 is about collective action, Oliver Stone's World Trade Center is about survival. Based on the experiences of Port Authority police officers trapped beneath the rubble, the film deliberately narrows the enormous geopolitical significance of 9/11 into the physical experience of two men trying to stay alive. Nicolas Cage and Michael Peña play officers John McLoughlin and Will Jimeno, whose world becomes darkness, concrete, pain and uncertainty.Stone, a filmmaker often associated with political controversy, does not make the film primarily about George W. Bush, terrorism or American foreign policy. Instead, he makes it about the human body confronting an almost unimaginable physical environment.The film's emotional power comes from the contrast between what is happening above ground and below it. Above ground is chaos; beneath the rubble is intimate human dependence. Survival becomes a shared act.Yet World Trade Center is also about the emotional culture of post-9/11 America. It emphasises sacrifice, courage, family and faith. It captures the desire of the period to find a reassuring narrative within an incomprehensible catastrophe.United 93 is deliberately austere, and World Trade Center is more conventional and sentimental. Two films released in the same year demonstrate two competing ways of remembering 9/11: one through almost unbearable realism, the other through the consolations of heroism and human resilience.Reign Over Me, Director: Mike Binder, 2007Reign Over Me is arguably more interesting today because it asks a question that the immediate post-9/11 culture could not easily ask: what happens after everyone else has moved on? Or, more importantly, it’s a film that goes into the heart of trauma. That is why the film is a must watch for people living in our times. No matter what the trauma, Reign Over Me does seem familiar to all of us.Adam Sandler plays Charlie Fineman, a man who lost his wife and daughters in the World Trade Center attacks. Years later, he has withdrawn almost completely from his former life. His old college friend Alan Johnson, played by Don Cheadle, encounters him and gradually tries to reconnect him with the world.The film does not attempt to recreate the attacks. Instead, 9/11 exists as an absence, an invisible force that has reorganised Charlie's entire personality. The trauma is not an event, rather its afterlife.Charlie is not simply grieving. He has become psychologically suspended in time. His refusal to remember is paradoxically the way he remembers. His isolation is a form of self-protection. Something we can all identify with in our post-pandemic reality.The friendship between Charlie and Alan gives the film its emotional architecture. Alan initially thinks he is helping Charlie, but gradually discovers that his own apparently successful life is also emotionally compromised. The film therefore avoids making trauma a condition that belongs only to the obvious victim. Everyone carries something. That is why this film is a must-watch.Reign Over Me also represents an early attempt to understand 9/11 through the lens of mental health and private grief rather than national identity. It isn’t about ‘How did America respond?’ but ‘How does one person survive when the future has become impossible to imagine?’Zero Dark Thirty, Director: Kathryn Bigelow, 2012If the earlier films ask what happened to people on September 11, Zero Dark Thirty asks what happened to America afterwards. Bigelow's film follows the decade-long hunt for Osama bin Laden, using the fictional composite CIA operative Maya as its central character. The film turns the pursuit into a procedural thriller, emphasising intelligence gathering, surveillance, interrogation and finally the Abbottabad raid.Its strength is its sense of institutional obsession. Maya's (Jessica Chastain) life becomes almost entirely organised around one objective. The passage of years is registered less through conventional personal development than through changing intelligence, political administrations and technological methods.But Zero Dark Thirty also remains controversial because of its treatment of torture. The film raises a disturbing question: does a society fighting a monstrous enemy begin to adopt methods that change its own moral identity?Bigelow does not make the question easy. The film is neither straightforward propaganda nor a conventional condemnation of the security state. Its clinical style is unsettling because it presents extraordinary violence through the “cool” language of procedure.The Report, Director: Scott Z. Burns, 2019The Report examines the machinery that made torture possible. Burns's film follows Senate investigator Daniel Jones, played by Adam Driver, as he investigates the CIA’s post-9/11 detention and interrogation programme. The resulting Senate investigation eventually produced a massive report documenting the programme and its consequences.What makes the film remarkable is that almost nothing about it looks traditionally cinematic. There are offices, documents, interviews, computer screens, corridors and endless arguments over language. Yet Burns turns bureaucracy into suspense.The film displays that the most consequential events in history, at times, do not happen in spectacular rooms or on battlefields. They happen in institutions, through memos, omissions, classified files and carefully chosen words.The film is also a corrective to the idea that the post-9/11 response can be understood only through military action. The “war on terror” was also a war fought inside legal and bureaucratic systems, where definitions of torture, national security and accountability were repeatedly contested.Daniel Jones’s persistence gives the film its moral centre. He is not an action hero. His weapon is documentation.That makes The Report particularly relevant 25 years later. Democracies depend on institutions capable of investigating themselves. The film asks what happens when those institutions protect themselves instead of democracy.The Reluctant Fundamentalist, Director: Mira Nair, 2012Nair’s The Reluctant Fundamentalist is an important film in this group for understanding how 9/11 looked from outside America. Riz Ahmed plays Changez Khan, a Pakistani graduate of Princeton, who builds a successful career on Wall Street. Before 9/11, he is deeply invested in the American dream. After the attacks, however, the identity he thought was his strength becomes the reason people look at him with suspicion.The film is fundamentally about belonging. Changez does not simply lose a job or a relationship. He loses the assumption that he can move comfortably between identities. His beard, Pakistani background and Muslim identity acquire political meaning that they did not previously possess.That’s how Nair's film expands the 9/11 conversation. The attacks created fear and new categories of suspicion. Muslims and South Asians in Western societies were often forced to negotiate an identity suddenly viewed through the prism of security — and judgement.The title is deliberately provocative. Who is the fundamentalist? The man who becomes disillusioned with America, or the society that begins to see an entire community through a narrow ideological lens?Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close, Director: Stephen Daldry, 2011Daldry's Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close takes one of the boldest perspectives possible: that of a child. Oskar, played by Thomas Horn, loses his father in the World Trade Center attacks. He discovers a mysterious key among his father's possessions and begins searching New York for the lock it might open.The quest is literal, but its real purpose is emotional. Oskar is trying to turn an incomprehensible tragedy into a puzzle that can be solved. That is what makes the film interesting. Children often process grief through objects, rituals and stories because abstract explanations are too difficult to comprehend.Oskar's search therefore becomes a metaphor for the human desire to impose order on catastrophe. The film also understands that grief is not linear. Oskar is angry, frightened, obsessive and sometimes emotionally difficult. His intelligence does not protect him from trauma.The presence of older generations, particularly the mysterious elderly man played by Max von Sydow, broadens the film’s idea of historical trauma. Oskar's grief is specifically 9/11, but the film suggests that human beings have always carried the consequences of violence.This film’s brilliance is that it is less a film about explaining 9/11 than about the impossibility of explaining it to someone who needs an answer.Remember Me, Director: Allen Coulter, 2010For most of its running time, the Robert Pattinson-led romantic drama is a story about damaged young people, family conflict, love and unresolved grief. It unfolds as an intimate portrait of people struggling to come to terms with loss and find meaning in their relationships. Yet the film has a larger historical context that gives its seemingly personal story a very different resonance, which is why Remember Me belongs on a list of films connected to 9/11.Worth, Director: Sara Colangelo, 2020Worth may be the quietest and, in some ways, the most mature film in this collection. Michael Keaton plays a lawyer, Kenneth Feinberg, appointed to administer the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. His task sounds administrative: determine how much money should be given to the families of those killed or injured.But the film understands the moral absurdity of the assignment. Because, really, how much is a life worth? The moment the question is converted into a number, the emotional contradiction becomes unavoidable. The government needs a formula. Families need recognition. Lawyers need consistency. Grieving people need justice. These demands cannot easily coexist.Sara Colangelo avoids turning the attacks themselves into spectacle. The towers are largely absent. The film is about conference rooms, arguments, spreadsheets, families and uncomfortable conversations. The horror exists in the spaces between people.The character of Charles Wolf, played by Stanley Tucci, is particularly important because he refuses to allow the victims to become statistics. His resistance forces Feinberg to understand that mathematical equality and emotional fairness are not the same thing.In that sense, Worth represents a major evolution in 9/11 cinema. The event has moved so far into the past that the question is no longer simply how people survived it. It is how institutions tried—and often failed—to deal with what remained.TV seriesThe Looming Tower, 2018Created by Dan Futterman, Alex Gibney and Lawrence Wright; directed across the series by Craig Zisk, John Dahl, Ali Selim, Michael Slovis and Alex GibneyMost 9/11 films begin on September 11, The Looming Tower begins years earlier. Based on Lawrence Wright's Pulitzer Prize-winning book, the 10-part miniseries reconstructs the rise of Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda during the 1990s while focusing on the increasingly bitter rivalry between the FBI and CIA. Jeff Daniels plays FBI counterterrorism chief John O’Neill, while Tahar Rahim plays FBI agent Ali Soufan.Its central insight is devastatingly simple: Most times, institutions fail because of ego. Because the people who possess different pieces of the truth fail to share them. The series turns bureaucratic rivalry into tragedy. The FBI and CIA are ostensibly pursuing the same enemy, yet competition over information, jurisdiction and institutional authority repeatedly gets in the way.That makes The Looming Tower fundamentally different from the other works here. The dramatic irony is relentless because the audience knows what the characters do not. Every warning sign becomes painful because we know where it leads.The final episodes are particularly powerful because the audience watches the machinery of disaster move into position while the characters remain trapped inside their institutional battles. The series’ final episode reaches September 11, but the real tragedy has already been constructed over the preceding decade.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Gen Z real estate influencers are selling homes on TikTok one joke at a time
articles.summary: Gen Z real estate agents know that glossy listing videos aren't enough to win over potential clients. Why not make a funny TikTok video instead?
articles.body:
Real estate influencers are here, and they want to sell you a home with a dance video.

Gen Z real estate agents are using social media to stand out from the competition.

Not everyone gets it — especially their elders — but it can pay off.

Merek Greene gives plenty of home tours IRL. But when the 24-year-old luxury real estate agent decided to post a virtual tour of one of his properties on TikTok this July, he gave the video a silly, topical spin.

Casting himself as a "Love Island" contestant who has just received a text about a listing, Greene describes the San Diego apartment as a new bombshell who "won't stay single for long."

"He's stunning, move-in ready, and turning heads," Greene says. "Let's see if this is your perfect match." The video ends with a callout to schedule a private showing.

A former theater kid and an agent with Compass in San Diego, Greene posts property tours, snippets of his daily life, dance videos, and real estate comedy sketches to his more than 19,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. As part of a generation that grew up online, he knows that social media is a powerful tool for his career — not just for translating listings into sales, but for building his brand and reputation to attract the attention of future clients.

But unlike the average agent posting self-serious slideshows of glossy listing photos, Greene is part of a cohort of Gen Z real estate agents making a name for themselves online with humor. The real estate content creators are here, and, to the chagrin of their more traditional elders, they're landing clients and making sales one joke and dance video at a time.

For Greene, having a presence on social media is a way to be more relatable to prospective clients.

"People may think of a Realtor as an old guy in a suit — not necessarily energetic or fun," Greene told me. He wants his followers and potential clients to see that he's a real human being — one who also "just sold a $2.1 million home."

"I'm building exposure," he said, comparing each video he makes to holding an open house. "I've gotten many referrals just by staying top of mind from posting. I think that's the biggest power of building your brand on social media and showing your authentic self."

It's paying off: Since 2022, he has closed more than $22 million in real estate deals.

In an unstable job market, real estate has become an increasingly popular career path for Gen Z, who are drawn to the opportunity to make serious cash outside a traditional 9-to-5. NAR's Member Profile shows that the share of Realtors under 30 rose from 1% in 2023 to 4% in 2024, before settling at 3% in 2025.

For these digital-native agents, TikTok and Instagram are important platforms for building a following. But with countless agents competing for attention in an endless scroll, standing out is paramount. One way to stand out is to make people laugh.

Tampa-based agent Breanna Banaciski, who describes herself as a "comedian disguised as a Realtor," roasts the homes she sells. In one tour, she jokes that Martha Stewart's jail cell was larger than the home's 800 square feet. Trenton Miller has built a following of more than 2 million with his comically nauseating high-speed home tours , while Maine agent Mitchell Tebo does literal backflips into lakes and rivers before showing properties.

"We're seeing more agents lean into humor, trends, and relatable moments because they know another 'Just Listed' post isn't necessarily going to stop someone from scrolling," said Katie Lance, a social media consultant who has taught real estate marketing online and at national conferences for nearly 20 years. "People do business with people they know, like, trust, and relate to, and humor is relatable."

Being funny online can pay off, but several agents told me there's a downside to making yourself part of the entertainment.

Toni Marmo, a former real estate agent from New Jersey, told me she faced judgment from coworkers for making fun of herself in her Reels. In one of her videos, she pokes fun at being a Gen Z realtor and pretends to be friends with a client, dropping Gen Z slang and references to "Love Island." The video received more than 247,000 likes and 14,400 shares on TikTok, but Marmo said not everyone in her office was a fan.

"It wasn't buyers, sellers, or anyone like that who was getting upset," Marmo said. "It was more other agents who were like, 'Who is this young girl making a fool out of herself, making a joke out of what we do?'"

MJ Maitland, a 25-year-old agent with eXp Realty from North Texas, told me no one at her brokerage has qualms about her content. In fact, her signature shtick — suddenly sprinting through gorgeous midcentury modern homes — has become so expected by her nearly 14,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok that she said they get mad when she doesn't run in her videos.

Still, Maitland said some agents outside her brokerage don't understand the bit.

"Honestly, thank goodness the agents that I've met in person have been great," she said. "But I've had not-so-great experiences with agents who just don't know me or get what I'm doing."

Social-media success can open the door to other career paths

After building a sizable following through her videos, Marmo left real estate in 2025 to be a full-time content creator . She now posts lifestyle and business videos aimed at helping her more than 70,000 TikTok and Instagram followers navigate their 20s.

Marmo, who's done deals with brands like Wawa, Dairy Queen, the skincare brand Tower 28, and the movie "The Devil Wears Prada 2," told me she now earns more from content creation than she ever did in real estate sales.

"Each paid brand deal brings in the equivalent of half to a whole real estate check," she said, adding that she's typically paid from $1,200 to $3,200 and above for a single brand deal, depending on the deliverables.

Marmo said other young agents are also starting to see posting online as a source of income — and, in some cases, a new career path.

"I see a lot of them realizing they can make just as much money from posting content," Marmo said. "I still get a ton of DMs from people who got into real estate and are struggling. They ask me how I transitioned out of the industry, and I think they follow my journey because it shows them that other options are possible."

For Maitland, expanding her online brand to incorporate her interests in architecture, history, and thrifting isn't about building an off-ramp to a different career. She plans to stay in real estate and appease her fans by sprinting around midcentury houses in Dallas, but emphasized that she doesn't want her page to be "sales-y."

"People want to see something more than just being an agent," she said. "Being funny is my niche. It works, so why not?"

articles.title: Students with President Bush on 9/11 look back on day: 'You could see it on his face'
articles.summary: Bush was visiting the school when he received news the nation was under attack.
articles.body:
Former Sarasota, Florida, second grade student Krystal Davis remembers a wave of confusion washing over her and her classmates on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001 , after a suited man whispered into the ear of the president of the United States, who was seated just in front of the students.

Then-President George W. Bush was visiting Emma E. Booker Elementary School and had been listening intently to the children in Mrs. Sandra Daniels' second-grade class flexing their reading skills, when the look of admiration on his face suddenly gave way to an expression of concern.

Chief of Staff Andrew Card had just relayed to Bush that a second plane had crashed into the World Trade Center in New York City. " America is under attack ," he later recalled whispering to the president.

9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.

"You could see the shift with [the president] once he got the message, and then you could see it on his face," Davis said in an interview with ABC News commemorating 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. "And then the shift of him going back to his normal self and smiling like, 'I don't want to alarm the kids.'"

Teacher Daniels told Sarasota ABC affiliate WWSB in an interview published Tuesday that she "immediately knew something was wrong" at that moment.

"His entire demeanor changed," she recalled, referring to Bush.

Davis described the concern among the students as Bush was escorted out of the room, once the reading lesson concluded.

"And we're just like, 'OK, in the middle of reading, what happened? What did we do? Like, did we do something wrong? Did he not like us reading or whatever?'" Davis recalled.

Though unaware at the time, Davis and her classmates had a front-row seat to history.

Meanwhile, 10-year-old Stevenson Tose'-Rigell, son of principal Gwendolyn Tose'-Rigell, was in the school's library eagerly awaiting the president's arrival, where Bush was slated to deliver a speech on his signature education policy, the No Child Left Behind Act.

"I'd probably say it was a couple of hours at least we were out there on the podium waiting around. We didn't know what was going on at the time," he said.

He continued, "They were trying to entertain us a little bit and, you know, keep, everybody feeling kind of excited … but we're waiting around for hours, you know, it's like, 'Man, this is this a long time waiting around for someone.'"

Tose'-Rigell said Bush did eventually enter the room, but the 10-year-old quickly realized the speech Bush was delivering would not touch on education policy. Instead, Bush delivered an address to the nation, confirming reports of "an apparent terrorist attack on our country."

"We're pretty much [thinking], 'Sounds like we're under attack,'" Tose'-Rigell recalled. "So yeah, it was definitely far off from the script."

Back in Daniels' classroom, Davis said the children were moved into another room, where a teacher tried to explain what was going on.

Davis said it was at that moment the students watched the images of the World Trade Center's Twin Towers crashing down on a television.

Tose'-Rigell said he was not able to leave school right away, as his mother was the school's principal. Instead, he said he watched the devastation unfold on a small TV in the school's front office.

From Sarasota, Bush boarded Air Force One, departing Florida for military bases in Louisiana and Nebraska before arriving back in Washington, D.C., that night.

By day's end, nearly 3,000 people had died in terror attacks at the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon building in Arlington, Virginia; and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93.

A quarter century later, as the country continues to grapple with the ramifications of that day, so too do the alumni of Emma E. Booker Elementary who were at the school the day of the attacks.

In May, the school commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 by welcoming a steel beam from the World Trade Center, brought by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, which allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day."

Stephen Siller Jr., whose father Stephen Siller was one of the 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11, said bringing the steel beam to Emma E. Booker Elementary was one of the most impactful visits he's made with the foundation's Steel Across America campaign, out of dozens of similar trips.

"Little kids ... understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history," he said. "...It once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day."

In a statement to ABC News, Sarasota County Schools Superintendent Terry Connor reflected on the impact 9/11 had on the district.

"For Sarasota County Schools, the legacy of Sept. 11 carries a uniquely personal connection," the statement read in part.

It added, "On this 25th anniversary, we honor those who were lost, remember those who answered the call, and express our gratitude to all who continue to serve our communities and our country."

Speaking with ABC News, the former students of Emma E. Booker Elementary reflected on their intersection with history, recognizing the grave impact on those directly affected by the tragedy while also considering the mark it left on their own lives.

"You realize, 'People really lost they live[s] yesterday,'" Davis said, recounting the days following 9/11. "And we were right in the midst of everything. [The president] was right here in Sarasota, Florida, [when it happened]."

Davis, who currently works in healthcare but said she aspires to be a police officer, said the events that day inspired her to pursue a career serving others.

"As a second grader, I couldn't really explain," Davis said, adding that she would later realize her experience left her "wanting to do more for my community, wanting to do more for myself and my kids."

"That day is going to always be something I never forget," she added.

Tose'-Rigell said he also carries complex feelings surrounding his memory of that day, including sadness and a sense of pride.

His mother, the school's former principal, died in 2007 after a battle with cancer.

"I always knew my mom was a rock star, you know? In my mind, you know, she was my superhero," Tose'-Rigell said, describing seeing his mother on the world stage on Sept. 11, 2001, and the "national recognition" she received.

He added that seeing her in archival footage from that day brought back memories of her each year on the anniversary of 9/11.

"It feels like she comes back," he said. "You know, like, once a year, [she] reincarnates right onscreen again."

articles.summary: A PF cumpriu 49 mandados de busca e apreensão em uma operação sobre os indícios de que o filme 'Dark Horse' recebeu dinheiro de emendas parlamentares.
articles.body:
Nesta quinta-feira (10), a Polícia Federal cumpriu 49 mandados de busca e apreensão em uma operação sobre os indícios de que o filme 'Dark Horse' recebeu dinheiro de emendas parlamentares. Entre os alvos estavam Karina Gama, produtora do filme, e o deputado federal Mario Frias (PL-SP) – o Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB) e a Academia Nacional de Cultura (ANC), presididos por Karina, também foram alvos. A Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU) apontou suspeita de desvio da emenda de R$ 2 milhões indicada por Frias para entidades de Karina. E a PF destacou ainda que a Go Up, empresa que produz o filme, movimentou R$ 19 milhões. articles.title: Drones formam silhueta das Torres Gêmeas em NY | G1
articles.standfirst: Homenagem utilizou milhares de drones para representar individualmente as pessoas mortas nos ataques de 2001.
articles.summary: Homenagem utilizou milhares de drones para representar individualmente as pessoas mortas nos ataques de 2001.
articles.body:
Um conjunto de 2.977 drones iluminou o céu do Porto de Nova York , nos Estados Unidos, nesta quarta-feira (9), para recriar o contorno das Torres Gêmeas do World Trade Center. Cada ponto de luz representou uma das vítimas dos ataques terroristas de 11 de setembro de 2001.

O espetáculo, chamado “2.977 Lights Over New York Harbor” , foi produzido por Addison Mehr em parceria com a empresa Sky Elements, com apoio da New York Foundation of the Arts. A apresentação ocorreu na véspera da data que marca os 25 anos dos atentados, lembrados nesta sexta-feira (11).

A proposta transformou os drones em uma espécie de constelação sobre o porto. Juntos, os pontos de luz formaram a silhueta das duas torres que faziam parte do horizonte de Nova York antes dos ataques.

Drones formam as Torres Gêmeas em homenagem ao 11 de setembro. — Foto: Reprodução/2977 Lights Over New York Harbor

O que aconteceu em 11 de setembro de 2001

Os ataques foram coordenados pela al-Qaeda e atingiram quatro alvos nos Estados Unidos.

Às 8h46, o primeiro avião atingiu a Torre Norte do World Trade Center. Dezessete minutos depois, às 9h03, um segundo avião colidiu contra a Torre Sul.

Um terceiro avião foi lançado contra o Pentágono, sede do Departamento de Defesa dos Estados Unidos.

O quarto avião caiu em uma área rural próxima a Shanksville, na Pensilvânia. O aparelho não chegou ao destino pretendido pelos sequestradores depois que passageiros reagiram e enfrentaram os criminosos.

Os ataques deixaram 2.977 vítimas, número que foi reproduzido pelo espetáculo de drones no céu de Nova York.

Drones formam as Torres Gêmeas em homenagem ao 11 de setembro. — Foto: Divulgação/Reuters

articles.title: A história do brasileiro que sobreviveu ao 11 de Setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Larry Pinto de Faria Jr. trabalhava no 25º andar da Torre Norte do World Trade Center, quando as Torres Gêmeas foram alvo de atentado terrorista em 11 de setembro de 2001. A data completa 25 anos nesta sexta-feira.
articles.summary: Larry Pinto de Faria Jr. trabalhava no 25º andar da Torre Norte do World Trade Center, quando as Torres Gêmeas foram alvo de atentado terrorista em 11 de setembro de 2001.
articles.body:
Larry Pinto de Faria Jr. em entrevista ao Globo Repórter de 14 de setembro de 2001 — Foto: Reprodução/Memória Globo

Um forte estrondo e um prédio de 110 andares estremecendo . Esse foi o primeiro impacto que o gaúcho Larry Pinto de Faria Jr. sentiu após um Boeing 767-200ER atingir a torre norte do World Trade Center, em Nova York , onde o economista trabalhava em 11 de setembro de 2001. A data completa 25 anos nesta sexta-feira (11).

Em um primeiro momento, ninguém sabia o que estava acontecendo. “Outra bomba no prédio”, reclamou um colega , lembrando de um ataque envolvendo um caminhão-bomba no estacionamento das Torres Gêmeas que ocorrera em 1993. De imediato, foi possível perceber que algo estava errado — mas ninguém no 25º andar imaginava a dimensão do atentado terrorista que mudaria o curso da humanidade.

“Pelo barulho que foi, pelo que balançou, bem que poderia ter sido uma bomba muito forte. Eu não tinha noção, naquele primeiro impacto”, lembra Larry.

“A descida foi muito tranquila, muito tranquila. Se as pessoas estavam muito assustadas? Olha, a descida me lembrou uma derrota do Inter no Beira-Rio. Descemos todos sem falar com ninguém, todo mundo quietinho, sem nenhuma pessoa passar na frente da outra. Não tinha pânico ”, completa.

Quando Larry chegou às ruas de Manhattan, o cenário era bem pior do que parecia inicialmente. Durante a descida, ele havia sido informado por um cliente que “um aviãozinho que bateu lá em cima”. Larry, contudo, percebe que algo maior estava em curso.

“Depois do impacto, eu disse para o meu chefe: vamos embora que isso vai cair. Não tem como um prédio desse tamanho aguentar o balanço que fez. Chegou a cair a caneta de cima da mesa. Foi um absurdo”, descreve.

Ao chegar no térreo, teve a confirmação de que se tratava de um avião de grande porte e que a torre sul também tinha sido atingida. E, então, a segunda torre que foi atingida cedeu, o arranha-céu veio a baixo e o pânico tomou conta .

“Medo mesmo, pavor, eu só tive em um momento. Quando eu saí caminhando, só olhei para cima e vi aquela torre grande caindo no meio dos escombros. Comecei a correr, porque estava muito próximo do prédio. Se tivesse caído na minha direção, eu teria morrido. Mas como ele caiu sobre si mesmo, só fui atingido por aquela nuvem de fumaça. Imagina: um prédio de 100 e tantos andares caindo e eu estava do lado dele.”

Outro momento de tensão foi quando Larry começou a se deslocar cada vez mais para o Sul da ilha de Manhattan, assim como todas as outras pessoas que estavam nos prédios que foram evacuados daquele lado das torres. Nesse momento, começaram a chegar informações sobre outros pontos dos Estados Unidos que estavam sob ataque, como o Pentágono, na capital Washington D.C.

“Eu já tinha escutado que tinham derrubado um avião na Pensilvânia. Tinha não sei quantos aviões que não sabiam onde estavam. Então, pensei, os caras estão atacando os Estados Unidos. Tem 10 mil pessoas aqui nessa praça onde estou. Se jogar um avião aqui, mata todo mundo. Era um formigueiro de gente”, lembra.

A torre norte foi atingida às 9h46 do horário local. A torre sul, às 10h03. Larry ficou mais de uma hora sem conseguir comunicar à família que estava bem e em segurança. Ao final do dia, consegui atravessar a Ponte do Brooklyn e chegar à sua casa em Nova Jersey, do outro lado do East River.

articles.title: Formação de ciclone traz tempestades ao RS nesta sexta-feira; previsão | G1
articles.standfirst: Áreas com maior potencial para chuvas severas são as regiões das Missões, Noroeste, Norte, Nordeste, Centro e Serra. Avisos do Inmet cobrem todo o estado.
articles.summary: Áreas com maior potencial para chuvas severas são as regiões das Missões, Noroeste, Norte, Nordeste, Centro e Serra. Avisos do Inmet cobrem todo o estado.
articles.body:
A formação de um ciclone , combinada a diferentes sistemas atmosféricos, cria condições favoráveis para temporais em praticamente todo o Rio Grande do Sul nesta sexta-feira (11). A previsão indica risco de granizo, chuva intensa e ventos que podem ultrapassar os 90 km/h .

Segundo a Climatempo Meteorologia, as áreas com maior potencial para ocorrência de tempestades severas são as regiões das Missões, Noroeste, Norte, Nordeste, Centro e Serra . Nesses locais, além da possibilidade de granizo de grande tamanho, os volumes de chuva podem variar entre 20 e 50 milímetros ao longo do dia, com acumulados pontuais que podem chegar a 90 milímetros.

O período de maior preocupação ocorre entre a madrugada e a manhã na metade Norte do estado. À tarde, as instabilidades também devem atingir com força áreas da Campanha e da Região Central.

Nas demais regiões, como Sul, Costa Doce, Vales, Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre e Litoral Norte, também há previsão de temporais isolados acompanhados de granizo.

Os alertas do Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) reforçam o cenário. O órgão emitiu avisos de tempestade válidos durante toda a sexta-feira para o Rio Grande do Sul . Além do alerta de perigo potencial (em amarelo) para todo o estado, há um aviso de perigo (em laranja) cobrindo grande parte do território gaúcho e um alerta de grande perigo (em vermelho) para áreas da Serra, do Noroeste e do Nordeste. Veja mapa abaixo.

Previsão de tempestade para sexta-feira (11) no RS — Foto: Divulgação/ Inmet

Depois da passagem do sistema mais intenso, o cenário muda gradualmente no sábado (12) . A chuva perde força, mas o céu continua carregado em muitas áreas do estado. Há possibilidade de garoa e chuva fraca , especialmente na metade Leste e na Campanha.

O destaque passa a ser a entrada de uma massa de ar frio . As temperaturas máximas devem ficar entre 9°C e 19°C, enquanto as mínimas previstas para a noite variam de 7°C a 13°C .

No domingo (13) , a atuação de um sistema de alta pressão deve garantir tempo estável na maior parte do Rio Grande do Sul. O amanhecer será marcado por frio mais intenso , principalmente na Serra e na Campanha.

As menores temperaturas previstas são de 7°C em municípios como Pinheiro Machado, São José dos Ausentes e Cambará do Sul. Já durante a tarde, o aquecimento será mais significativo no Noroeste, onde cidades como Iraí podem alcançar 23°C.

Ainda pode haver chuva fraca e isolada em áreas do Leste e próximas ao Litoral , mas com baixos volumes e de forma bastante localizada.

articles.summary: Comunidade rural de Marcela recebe Ação Integrada.
articles.body:
O Município de Montes Claros promoveu mais uma edição da Ação Integrada, evento que reúne todas as secretarias municipais e uma ampla gama de parceiros com o objetivo de aproximar os órgãos públicos da comunidade, fortalecendo o diálogo, a cidadania e o acesso a direitos essenciais, oferecendo serviços e atendimentos gratuitos, além de atividades educativas para a população.

Desta vez, a Ação Integrada foi realizada na comunidade rural de Marcela, na Escola Municipal Artur Fagundes de Oliveira. A banda CCZ Music, formada por servidores do Centro de Controle de Zoonoses, foi a responsável para animar os presentes com vários estilos musicais.

O servidor público municipal, pedagogo e artista Jean Santana também foi destaque na Ação Integral, ao apresentar seu teatro. Caracterizado de forma divertida como um mosquito da dengue, ele buscou conscientizar a comunidade sobre a importância de eliminar lugares com água parada para prevenir a multiplicação do inseto.

A Ação Integrada ofereceu serviços gratuitos e atividades educativas para todas as idades — Foto: Solon Queiroz

Durante o evento foram oferecidos diversos serviços, como atualização de dados no Cadastro Único (CadÚnico); agendamentos para emissão de RG e da Carteirinha da Pessoa Autista; e atendimentos realizados pelo Centro de Referência de Assistência Social (CRAS), Centro de Referência Especializado de Assistência Social (CREAS) e Centro de Atendimento à Mulher (CRAM).

Além disso, foram realizados os serviços gratuitos de corte de cabelo, elaboração de tranças, design de sobrancelhas e manicure; orientação sobre Carteirinha do Idoso; emissão do CAF (Cadastro Nacional da Agricultura Familiar); atendimento e orientação para produtores rurais; vacinação de cães e gatos; projeto Desenrola Rural; doação de mudas; orientações sobre programa habitacional popular; atividades esportivas e recreativas; além de orientações jurídicas e mediações para processos de casamento civil, divórcio, guarda, entre outros.

O agricultor familiar Juventino Barbosa elogiou a ação: “uma maravilha” — Foto: Solon Queiroz

O agricultor familiar Juventino Barbosa da Silva, morador de Marcela, aprovou a Ação Integrada: “essa ação está sendo uma maravilha para nossa comunidade e é algo inédito por aqui. Aproveitei a oportunidade para usar vários serviços”.

Emerson Lopes, da comunidade de Tiririca, aproveitou para conferir a pressão: “iniciativa da Prefeitura é muito positiva” — Foto: Solon Queiroz

Outro agricultor familiar, Emerson Lopes da Silva, morador da comunidade de Tiririca, também elogiou a ação. “Essa iniciativa da Prefeitura é muito positiva, oferecendo a oportunidade para acessar várias coisas, inclusive regularizar documentos e até fazer um check-up. Eu mesmo já verifiquei minha pressão arterial e está ótima”, relatou Emerson.

O casal Matheus e Giovana selou sua união dentro da Ação Integrada — Foto: Solon Queiroz

O casal residente na comunidade de Marcela, Matheus Henrique Gonçalves de Oliveira e Giovana Ribeiro Gonçalves, aproveitou a Ação Integral para trocar alianças. Além deles, diversos outros casais também oficializaram seus relacionamentos durante o evento.

“A Ação Integral é uma iniciativa crucial para disseminar informações entre os moradores da zona rural, como em Marcela, sobre os diversos benefícios que o Município oferece para a população do campo. Além disso, a ação também permite realizar e atualizar cadastros”, destacou Elwira Daphinn Moreira Guimarães, coordenadora da Agricultura Familiar do Município de Montes Claros.

Segundo Giovana Rocha, coordenadora de Proteção Social Básica da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Social, a Ação de Cidadania, implementada pela administração municipal, demonstra o compromisso de Montes Claros em implementar políticas públicas voltadas para toda a comunidade. O programa proporciona atenção, respeito e oportunidades de reinício, além de levar cidadania aos moradores e promover maior dignidade para todos.

articles.body:
Fumaça avança pelas ruas de Nova York após colapso de uma das torres do World Trade Center, em 11 de setembro de 2001 — Foto: Reuters

O ataque terrorista às Torres Gêmeas de Nova York, em 11 de setembro de 2001, completou 25 nesta sexta-feira (11).

Mesmo em uma época ainda sem smart phones ou redes sociais disseminados, as imagens do momento em que aviões comerciais bateram nos arranha-céus, que posteriormente desabaram, rodaram e chocaram o mundo.

Ainda assim, até hoje há imagens raras e ângulos pouco vistos do episódio. Veja, abaixo, algumas delas:

O atentado foi reivindicado pela rede terrorista Al-Qaeda. Terroristas do grupo sequestraram aviões em diferentes pontos do espaço aéreo dos Estados Unidos.

Dois deles se chocaram contra as Torres Gêmeas. Outro atingiu parte do Pentágono, a sede militar dos EUA, e um quarto foi derrubado na Pensilvânia, após passageiros se rebelarem contra os terroristas na aeronave.

No total, mais de 2.900 pessoas morreram, segundo autoridades.

articles.title: Sucessão de estragos com chuvas em menos de 2 meses deixa cidade de SP apreensiva: 'Famílias estão abaladas' | G1
articles.standfirst: Guariba, na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP), suspendeu aulas na rede municipal enquanto ainda se recupera de devastação causada por vendaval no fim de julho.
articles.summary: Guariba, na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP), suspendeu aulas na rede municipal enquanto ainda se recupera de devastação causada por vendaval no fim de julho.
articles.body:
Quase dois meses após a devastação causada por um severo temporal no interior de São Paulo, Guariba (SP) volta a enfrentar transtornos causados pela chuva.

Ainda se recuperando dos estragos do fim de julho, quando 70% das casas foram afetadas e houve queda generalizada na rede elétrica, a cidade de 37,4 mil habitantes a região de Ribeirão Preto (SP) agora lida com problemas nas escolas municipais, que tiveram aulas suspensas até o fim desta semana devido a infiltrações e danos ocasionados nas unidades.

Além dos prejuízos estruturais, essa sucessão de transtornos deixa a população em alerta constante.

"Todas as famílias guaribenses estão abaladas com essa força da natureza, então todos estão emocionalmente abalados, que qualquer vento, qualquer chuvinha, nós já ficamos muito preocupados", afirma a secretária municipal de Educação, Vera Eliana Ambrósio Politi.

Em 24 de julho, um temporal com ventos de até 160 km/h deixou um rastro de destruição em pelo menos seis cidades da região de Ribeirão Preto, que tiveram reconhecido pelo governo federal o estado de emergência.

Chuva causa alagamento em ruas de Guariba, SP — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Município mais afetado, Guariba ficou com 16 mil imóveis, o equivalente a 99% do total, sem eletricidade devido à queda de torres de transmissão. Segundo o prefeito Mançano Junior (PSD), em torno de 70% das casas foram danificadas e o parque industrial foi destruído.

A prefeitura precicou improvisar abrigos e uma cozinha industrial para atender os moradores que perderam tudo. As aulas na rede municipal também chegaram a ser suspensas. Um conjunto de estragos que, segundo uma estimativa inicial das autoridades, demandaria um aporte de R$ 50 milhões para obras de reconstrução no município.

"Todo local que havia um uma quadra coberta foi embora. Está retorcido. Nós tínhamos um grande galpão (...) galpão do agronegócio, não sobrou nada, mas nada mesmo", lamentou o prefeito na época, durante uma reunião com autoridades políticas da região.

Sete semanas depois, a cidade teve o restabelecimento da energia elétrica, mas ainda trabalha para se recuperar de todos os estragos.

Em meio a esse cenário de reconstrução, uma chuva na madrugada desta quinta-feira (10) causou estragos em diferentes escolas. Vídeos mostram unidades de ensino básico tomadas pela água. Parte do teto do refeitório de uma das escolas cedeu.

"A diretora, a coordenadora, os professores, funcionários, foram retirando os alunos das salas que estavam mais atingidas, que estavam com goteiras muito grandes, foram levando para as outras salas, remanejando salas que não estavam chovendo, que não havia gotejamento, para eles ficarem com maior segurança dentro da escola", descreveu a secretária.

Aulas da rede municipal de ensino de Guariba, SP, são suspensas após temporal — Foto: Redes sociais

Todas as aulas foram suspensas para cinco mil alunos até sexta-feira, quando equipes da Prefeitura vão tentar consertar os estragos para a volta às aulas na segunda-feira (14).

"Tem uma força-tarefa. A Secretaria de Obras está trabalhando desde ontem [quarta-feira]. Desde ontem ela já vem trabalhando para poder recuperar, desentupir calha, ver onde tem que substituir telha e assim por diante", disse o prefeito.

Desde o temporal de julho, moradores relatam um sentimento de apreensão permanente para os riscos causados por eventos climáticos.

"Cada vez mais as pessoas estão se surpreendendo. Quando começa a chover, as pessoas ficam mais assustadas ainda, por causa daquela outra chuva que deu aquele desastre. (...) Começou a ventar, as pessoas já ficam inseguras", afirma o vigilante Junior Alves.

Entre as autoridades, essa apreensão já se reflete em medidas como planos de reposição de aulas e de recomposição de aprendizagem, com atividades no contraturno escolar, para garantir que o calendário escolar não seja afetado por desastres, ainda mais com a chuva mais recente.

"Desde que aconteceu essa intempérie no nosso município, nós já temos um plano de reposição para que as crianças não tenham o seu rendimento prejudicado. (...) Nós já estamos elaborando um outro plano para alteração do calendário escolar de 2026.", afirma a secretária de Educação.

🌀Os ciclones extratropicais são sistemas de baixa pressão atmosférica – regiões causadoras de tempo adverso em grande escala – que surgem normalmente em latitudes médias. Eles são formados pelo contraste de temperaturas de diferentes massas de ar (quente e fria).

De acordo com a Climatempo, norte de Santa Catarina, todo o estado do Paraná, sul de São Paulo e sul do Mato Grosso do Sul podem registrar o fenômeno. (veja no mapa abaixo)

Entre quarta (9) e quinta-feira (10), os tornados já causaram estragos em algumas cidades do Paraná . Os fenômenos atingiram os municípios de Francisco Alves, no noroeste do estado, e Espigão Alto do Iguaçu, no oeste.

Na sexta, a abrangência do fenômeno pode ser maior porque o ciclone se soma a uma atmosfera já bastante instável.

Segundo os meteorologistas, dois fatores já vinham contribuindo para manter o tempo chuvoso no Centro-Sul e aumentar a chance da formação de tornados:

Uma corrente de ar mais quente e úmida que vem do Norte do Brasil , passa por áreas do Centro-Oeste e chega em áreas do Paraná, que favorece as instabilidades na região.

Presença de uma circulação de ventos conhecida como cavado , de cerca de cinco quilômetros de altura, que favorece a formação de nuvens muito carregadas.

🌧️Cavados são áreas alongadas de baixa pressão. Esse fenômeno meteorológico acontece quando há uma corrente de vento que ajuda na formação de nuvens de tempestade .

Esses dois componentes são essenciais para a configuração do que os meteorologistas chamam de supercélula.

"A supercélula é uma nuvem de tempestade muito grande mesmo que, pelas características de sua formação, pode dar origem aos tornados", detalha César Soares, meteorologista da Climatempo.

⛈️Em resumo, a supercélula é uma tempestade que apresenta uma corrente de ar em rotação no interior da nuvem. Esse tipo de formação pode gerar chuva forte, granizo, ventania e tornados.

Os meteorologistas ainda detalham que a atmosfera precisa reunir alguns componentes específicos para que esse tipo de nuvem seja formada:

Muita disponibilidade de umidade, em várias camadas da atmosfera

Grandes diferenças de velocidade e de direção do vento entre a superfície e as camadas médias e altas da atmosfera – condição que impulsiona o giro das nuvens

Condições favoráveis para impulsionar um grande desenvolvimento vertical das nuvens

Além de aumentar a chance de formação de tornados, o ciclone e, posteriormente, a frente fria devem manter o tempo instável em boa parte do Centro-Sul nesta sexta-feira (11).

⚠️Esses locais têm aviso de grande perigo para tempestades nesta sexta, com previsão de mais de 100 milímetros de chuva por dia e ventos superiores a 100 km/h . Também há risco de alagamentos e queda de árvores.

A sexta-feira será de tempo instável no Sul e no Sudeste , com chuva, trovoadas e possibilidade de temporais em diferentes áreas. No Norte e no Nordeste , as pancadas devem acontecer principalmente em áreas litorâneas e os o interior deve contar com períodos de sol e calor.

No Norte , o Amazonas concentra as principais áreas de instabilidade, com chuva e trovoadas no norte do estado. Também podem acontecer pancadas isoladas no centro-sul amazonense, oeste de Roraima, norte de Rondônia, norte e leste do Amapá e litoral do Pará. Tocantins e grande parte do Pará terão predomínio de sol e poucas nuvens.

No Nordeste , as chuvas ficam concentradas principalmente no litoral, atingindo áreas da Bahia, Sergipe, Alagoas, Rio Grande do Norte, Ceará, Piauí e Maranhão.

O interior da região terá maior presença de sol, especialmente no centro-sul maranhense, Piauí, sul do Ceará, oeste da Paraíba, centro-oeste de Pernambuco e norte e oeste da Bahia. Nas demais áreas, o céu fica mais nublado, sem previsão de chuva.

No Centro-Oeste , Mato Grosso do Sul terá o tempo mais instável, com chuva e trovoadas no centro-sul e leste do estado. Goiás também pode registrar chuva, principalmente no extremo sul.

A nebulosidade aumenta no centro goiano e no Distrito Federal, enquanto Mato Grosso terá predomínio de sol em boa parte do território.

O Sudeste também terá um dia de chuva. São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e o sul de Minas Gerais e do Espírito Santo podem registrar períodos chuvosos acompanhados de trovoadas.

No Triângulo Mineiro, em Belo Horizonte e em Vitória, a previsão é de pancadas isoladas. Nas demais áreas, o céu fica nublado, mas sem chuva.

No Sul , a instabilidade será generalizada. A previsão indica chuva, trovoadas, rajadas de vento e granizo, além da possibilidade de tempestades. O ambiente também favorece a formação de linhas de instabilidade e supercélulas.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Day that changed the world forever' and 'Mayors plot holiday tax'
articles.summary: A levy on overnight stays in England and Wales, 9/11 anniversary and Dame Esther Rantzen lead Friday's papers.
articles.body:
Many of the papers lead on the government's plans to introduce a tourist tax in England. The Guardian describes it as "a hammer blow" for the hotel industry. But it says some regional mayors have welcomed the proposals.

The Daily Mail says Andy Burnham has been accused of launching another raid on struggling families. "Welfare party strikes again," it says on its front page. According to the Daily Telegraph, the founder of the pub chain, JD Wetherspoon, said the plans would likely lead to higher prices across the hospitality sector. The Sun says working people have been "whacked" and asks "what the hol, PM?".

The Daily Mirror leads with the words of the assisted dying campaigner, Dame Esther Rantzen, who says her cancer has left her too frail now to travel to Dignitas . The headline is "It's too late for me". The Daily Star says the TV presenter is pleading with MPs to pass the assisted dying bill . A terminally ill mother interviewed in the Daily Express calls on ministers to "just pass the bill".

The Metro leads on the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 attacks. Its front page simply reads '9/11' . "The day that changed the world," reads the i newspaper's front page - which features a picture of a firefighter standing in the rubble of the fallen towers.

Household energy bills could increase by more than a £100 by the end of the decade , according to the front page of the Times. It says delays to new power lines -- needed to hit the government's clean power pledge - are to blame. A spokesperson for Neso, the government-owned body in charge of keeping Britain's lights on, said it was doing everything it could to keep costs down.

The Sun says the crew of an RAF Chinook helicopter was seen landing in the grounds of a luxury hotel on the shores of Loch Lomond , before leaving with cakes and other treats. An RAF source said hotel staff unexpectedly provided food during the planned stop. The paper dubs the airmen "the royal eclair force".

images.caption: Several of Friday's papers lead on the news that from early 2028, local mayors in England will be able to impose a tourist tax. The Guardian notes that the move has been "welcomed" by regional leaders, but ministers are facing "outrage" from the hospitality industry, which it says was expecting much stricter controls on how much could be charged and how the money will be used.

articles.title: Franklin Graham calls on America to 'turn back' to God 25 years after 9/11: 'We still need His help today'
articles.summary: Franklin Graham urges America to rediscover the faith that filled churches after 9/11 as the nation marks 25 years since the terrorist attacks.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Rev. Franklin Graham is calling on Americans to remember the extraordinary turn toward faith that followed the 9/11 terrorist attacks and to "turn back" to God as the nation marks 25 years since the day that changed the world forever. "September 11 is a day I’ll never forget," Graham, president and CEO of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association (BGEA) and Samaritan’s Purse, told Fox News Digital. "It’s impossible to describe the tremendous amount of pain that I witnessed at Ground Zero in the aftermath. There were so many who were in shock and grieving," he added. "It is still hard to fathom the depths of evil that caused so much destruction." As Americans commemorate a quarter-century since the attacks, Graham said his prayer is for America to rediscover her reliance on faith he witnessed in the aftermath. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS "As we observe the 25th anniversary of this day when our world changed forever, my prayer is that America will recognize our need for God like we did after 9/11," Graham said. "Churches were full. People gathered to pray in public places." Graham also recalled his father, the late evangelist Rev. Billy Graham, addressing the country from Washington National Cathedral during a national day of prayer and remembrance following the attacks. "We’ve always needed God from the very beginning of this nation. But today we need Him especially," Billy Graham said at the time, according to Graham’s statement. "We’re involved in a new kind of warfare. And we need the help of the Spirit of God." GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS "Just as America needed the help of God then, we still need His help today," Franklin Graham said. Those themes are at the center of BGEA’s new 30-minute program, "A Day That Changed Our Lives Forever," hosted by Graham and featuring survivors reflecting on the attacks and the faith and hope they say emerged from the devastation. Among them is Genelle Guzman-McMillan, the last person pulled alive from the World Trade Center rubble. Guzman-McMillan spent 27 hours buried beneath the ruins, unable to move and unsure whether she would survive. While trapped, she said she began thinking about her late mother and crying out to God for forgiveness and a second chance. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE At one point, Guzman-McMillan said she could no longer endure it. "God, are you listening to me? Please show me a sign," she recalled saying. Then something happened she still cannot explain. "And then someone grabbed me by my hand," Guzman-McMillan says in the special. "He told me his name is Paul." She said Paul held her hand and reassured her. SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE "You’re gonna be fine. Help is on the way. I’m not gonna let you go," she recalled him saying. As Guzman-McMillan began hearing rescuers’ radios, she said Paul encouraged her to keep calling out. Eventually, she heard a rescuer say, "I see her." "I just knew I was going to go home," she said. "I am the last survivor, buried for 27 hours. I myself couldn’t believe that I survived it." Guzman-McMillan said she believes the mysterious Paul was "an angel looking out for me." "I wasn’t hallucinating, I wasn’t dreaming," she said. "I knew the conversation that I had." I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES "Something happened under that rubble," she added. "I found Jesus that day." The special features another dramatic survival story from Sujo John, a father-to-be who worked on the 81st floor of the North Tower while his pregnant wife worked on the 71st floor of the South Tower. After escaping, he spent hours believing his wife had died. Then his cellphone rang. "I picked up that call thinking this is going to be the worst news of my life," he recalled. 9/11 HERO’S MEMORY PRESERVED THROUGH MASSIVE EFFORT TO ‘DO GOOD’ FOR VETS, FIRST RESPONDERS: ‘HIS LEGACY’ His wife was on the other end. She had been late for work by just minutes. "She thought I was dead," he said. The two arranged a meeting place and ran toward each other. "We both survived." Graham also recounted traveling to New York after the attacks and seeing people holding photographs of missing loved ones and desperately seeking information. He began calling pastors and asking them to come help comfort and pray with grieving families. FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' — THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE That response ultimately led Graham to form the Billy Graham Rapid Response Team, which BGEA says has grown into an international network of thousands of crisis-trained chaplains who minister to people facing emotional and spiritual needs following tragedies and disasters. Graham hosts "A Day That Changed Our Lives Forever," airing on Fox News Channel at 12:30 a.m. ET. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Twenty-five years later, Graham said his prayer for America remains clear. "My prayer for our nation is that we will turn back to the God of Heaven who has brought us to this day and sustained us every step of the way."

articles.title: Ms Rachel defends 'awesome' Mamdani amid 9/11 memorial controversy, says he's victim of Islamophobic attacks
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani drew praise from children's influencer Ms. Rachel amid fierce backlash over his ties to terror sympathizers before the 9/11 25th anniversary memorial.
articles.body: Left-wing children’s influencer Ms. Rachel praised New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani amid a controversy over whether he should attend the 9/11 memorial on its 25th anniversary. Political rancor is threatening to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not attend. Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Accurso, appeared to address the controversy on the eve of the memorial in a social media post on Instagram, writing in a statement, "Mayor Mamdani is awesome. I’ve met him, and he truly cares about New Yorkers. He’s such a kind, gentle soul. Our NYC Pre-K curriculum teaches children to be kind, respect different religions and cultures, and be proud of who they are. "It’s unacceptable that adults still judge, hate and attack each other because of religion and skin color. We should be setting a better example for our children." 9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD She added further in a caption to the post, "Also so disappointing to see some Christians expressing hate and Islamophobia. Jesus was Jewish, and he taught us in the Good Samaritan parable that our neighbors are not just those who share our religion." There has been widespread controversy about Mamdani being associated with any 9/11 memorials based on his own politics and that of his associates. An online petition led by family members of people killed on Sept. 11 — signed by over 100,000 people — has called on Mamdani to skip the memorial. "Mr. Mamdani has praised Brooklyn Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has been linked to radical Islam, was named as an alleged co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, and served as a character witness for the 'Blind Sheikh,' who was convicted in 1995 of plotting terror attacks against the United States," the petition said. "Mr. Mamdani has endorsed candidates such as Aber Kawas, who described 9/11 as an attack 'a couple of people did in the context of U.S. capitalism, racism, White supremacy, and Islamophobia,' and who also expressed sympathy for Ahmed Ferhani, who pleaded guilty to plotting to blow up a Manhattan synagogue," it added. Mamdani and other socialist candidates' association with far-left activist Hasan Piker has also gotten intense scrutiny over Piker's past comments that the United States "deserved" the attacks, remarks he promptly walked back at the time but continue to haunt him and his political circle. Mamdani has also condemned the comment. HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE Mamdani has faced backlash for giving a ceremonial pen from a 9/11 remembrance ceremony to a top aide who once represented a convicted al Qaeda member. Mamdani had handed the pen to his chief counsel, Ramzi Kassem. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships and was the brother-in-law of Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon, killing 184. Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office and did not receive an immediate response. articles.body: BENGALURU: “I killed them because I loved them and was worried about their future,” SG Imran told investigators after allegedly strangling his two young daughters at a hotel near Kempegowda International Airport last month.The 40-year-old manager at a local cab company broke down during a recent police reconstruction of the crime inside the hotel room, weeping uncontrollably and rolling on the floor for nearly 20 minutes as he lamented the deaths of Shaik Zoya, 10, and Shaik Zehara, 5.Imran, a resident of Bilalnagar, allegedly killed the girls on August 10 before attempting to take his own life by slitting his throat. He was shifted to a private hospital and recovered in about two weeks.During the reconstruction, police said Imran collapsed to the floor and continued sobbing. “We did not stop him or try to pacify him. We knew that he had to pour out his feelings. He wept, cried, and lamented for around 15–20 minutes, and we just watched him,” said a senior police officer handling the investigation.During interrogation, Imran admitted to the double murder and told investigators that he had been overcome by fears about his daughters’ upbringing following the breakdown of his marriage.According to police, Imran said his marriage began deteriorating around 15 months ago after his wife got a new job. He alleged that he discovered WhatsApp conversations between her and a male colleague, leading to frequent domestic disputes and eventually their separation two months before the killings.Under an informal arrangement, the children stayed with their mother on weekdays and visited Imran on weekends.Police also recovered a suicide note from the hotel room in which Imran allegedly wrote about his wife’s alleged infidelity, marital discord and the custody dispute.Police said Imran sometimes experiences mood swings. articles.title: 'They blew the hell out of Bahrain': US official admits Iran damaged US base
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US Navy is assessing what to do with its key base in Bahrain after Iranian strikes caused extensive damage to the facility, with a senior US offic.
articles.body: The US Navy is assessing what to do with its key base in Bahrain after Iranian strikes caused extensive damage to the facility, with a senior US official acknowledging the scale of the attack, The Hill reported, citing local media.“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” Cao said in an interview with The Epoch Times, published Thursday, referring to Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NASB), the headquarters of US Naval Forces Central Command and the US Fifth Fleet.The base has been heavily targeted by Iran since the US and Israel launched airstrikes against the Islamic Republic in late February. NASB serves as a major logistics hub for the US Navy's operations in the Middle East.Cao said the Navy was now considering its options for the facility, including whether it should be repaired. “I have a task force that’s looking at that,” he told the publication.The extent of the damage has already raised questions over when US forces can return to the base. In late August, Chief of Naval Operations Adm Daryl Caudle said sailors would not be returning anytime soon, including to retrieve their personal belongings.“We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” Caudle said during a town hall on August 31. “I just want to be completely honest with that.”The damage to the Bahrain facility comes amid a wider escalation between the US and Iran, with American military assets across the region coming under attack.Multiple US aircraft were damaged in a separate Iranian ballistic missile strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, CBS News reported, citing sources. An A-10 Thunderbolt was reportedly left with a missing wing, while around eight F-15 fighter jets suffered light damage but were later returned to service. US forces fired more than 30 Patriot missiles during the attack.Iranian forces have also targeted US naval assets and shipping interests as the conflict has intensified. The latest escalation followed US strikes on five Iranian oil tankers, with US President Donald Trump confirming Washington's role and warning of further attacks.The conflict has also put pressure on vital energy and shipping routes. The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, while Iran-aligned Houthi forces have expanded operations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, raising fresh concerns over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and global oil supplies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Patrol sergeant accused of murdering sheriff’s captain in yearslong romantic dispute over woman they dated
articles.summary: Sgt. Nekime Matu Oxendine is accused of fatally shooting Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean after a confrontation outside a woman’s home.
articles.body: A North Carolina highway patrol sergeant has been indicted in the murder of a sheriff’s captain following a years-long romantic dispute involving a woman both officers dated, according to authorities. North Carolina State Highway Patrol Sgt. Nekime Matu Oxendine, 44, reportedly shot Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean on March 27 outside the woman’s home in Hope Mills following a confrontation between the two men, according to authorities and CityView. Police arrived to find the woman, Tara Lynn Whitman, performing CPR on Bean as Oxendine remained nearby, according to search warrant filings. Bean was pronounced dead at the scene, officials said. The fatal shooting followed years of escalating tension surrounding Whitman’s relationships with both men, state investigators wrote in court filings. FORMER COLLEAGUES DETAIL CHP CAPTAIN’S SPIRAL BEFORE ALLEGED MURDER-FOR-HIRE PLOT AGAINST HUSBAND According to investigators, Oxendine had displayed persistent jealousy and insecurity over the years regarding Whitman’s connection to Bean. According to the warrant, Whitman began dating Bean in 2022 after ending a long-term relationship with Oxendine. She eventually ended that relationship and returned to Oxendine. FLORIDA DEPUTY KILLED EX-GIRLFRIEND OVER A TV, THEN HIMSELF, SHERIFF SAYS While Whitman was with Bean, Oxendine appeared to exhibit increasingly concerning behavior, according to text messages cited in the warrant. Whitman and Bean had described some of his behavior as "stalking," documents reported. "I seen u have been talking to Adam!!! Best wishes!!!" Oxendine wrote in one message. "Better tell that Mother F—er to get ready too!!! " he added. Oxendine also sent messages questioning Whitman’s decision to stay with Bean, demanding to know the truth and claiming he knew where Bean lived, according to the warrant. In December 2025, Whitman eventually resumed her romantic relationship with Oxendine, moving out of the home she shared with Bean. For the next three months, however, Oxendine continued to show insecurity over Bean, asking Whitman whether Bean was more attractive and accusing him of having the power to "lure u in and out of my life on demand." He also sought continued reassurance about Whitman’s commitment, according to the warrant Then, on the night of March 27, Bean asked Whitman to come to his residence after work to talk. Whitman initially agreed but later stopped responding to his messages. When Whitman did not show up, Bean messaged her, "F— it, I’ll come to you," and threatened to blow his car horn and cause a scene if she did not come outside. When Bean arrived, he became irate after seeing Oxendine’s vehicle parked outside, according to the warrant. Oxendine stepped outside and fired about two warning shots into the ground. Bean continued advancing toward him, and Oxendine then opened fire two to three more times, according to the warrant. Bean collapsed onto his back in the yard, according to the warrant. Police said they found a handgun and magazine nearby. Oxendine has been charged with first-degree murder. He was posthumously recognized with the Merit Award for his outstanding service, forward-thinking leadership, initiative and lasting contributions to the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office.
