articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Hong Kong court is set to sentence on Friday three activists who spent years organising public gatherings to remember the 1989 Tiananmen Square mass.
articles.body: A Hong Kong court is set to sentence on Friday three activists who spent years organising public gatherings to remember the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre in China.Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung and Albert Ho were convicted earlier this year of inciting subversion under the national security law imposed by Beijing. They could each face up to 10 years in prison.The case is being closely watched because it tests how much space remains for dissent in Hong Kong, where authorities have sharply restricted public protests, elections and critical media since the 2019 unrest.Activists face sentencingThe three defendants led the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China. For three decades, the group organised a large annual gathering in Victoria Park to remember those killed when Chinese troops crushed pro-democracy protests in Beijing in 1989.The event drew tens of thousands of people each year and was the only major public commemoration of the crackdown held in China. Authorities banned it in 2020, citing the coronavirus pandemic.In August, three government-approved judges found the activists guilty after ruling that the alliance’s call to “end one-party dictatorship” encouraged people to overthrow or undermine the Chinese Communist Party.Lee and Chow pleaded not guilty, while Ho admitted the charge. The three were arrested in September 2021 and have remained in custody for years.The defence argued that the alliance had not called for violence or any unlawful action. Lee said the demand to “end one-party dictatorship” simply meant allowing people to choose their leaders through democratic means.Chow, who represented herself in court, said the verdict showed that pursuing democracy had become a crime and that she did not deserve even one day in prison.Hong Kong freedoms under pressureHong Kong once had a strong civil society, regular mass protests and a relatively open press. Since the 2019 protest movement, however, the authorities have restricted political participation and prosecuted prominent activists and media figures.Several civil society groups have shut down, including the alliance behind the Tiananmen gatherings. In February, former pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai was sentenced to 20 years in prison under the security law.Beijing says the legislation is needed to protect stability. China's foreign ministry office in Hong Kong said the city was governed by the rule of law and that nobody could engage in unlawful activities under the pretext of “freedom of speech and press".Critics argue that the trial shows peaceful demands for political change are now being treated as criminal acts.Urania Chiu, a law lecturer at Oxford Brookes University in the UK, said the convictions confirmed that even peaceful calls for democratic change in China are now criminalised in Hong Kong.People queued outside the court ahead of Friday’s hearing. Simon Ng, who attended the vigils for years, said the case had affected him personally.“I took part in the alliance's vigils for decades, the ruling amounts to an accusation against me,” he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: KANPUR: Five days after pharmaceutical trader Vineet Manocha was stabbed to death inside his Kanpur home, questions over who knew about the alleged murder plot have brought his son Subrat Manocha under scrutiny.The main focus of the investigation remains Subrat's wife, Shalu Manocha, whom police allege helped plan the murder and enlisted two alleged contract killers, Vishal Gautam and Raj Kishore.Shalu's family, however, has rejected the allegations. Her elder brother Dheeraj Arora and sister Sonia Mehrotra told reporters on Thursday that it was difficult to believe she could have orchestrated the killing.Arora said Shalu was close to Vineet and regularly looked after his food and other daily needs. He also questioned why Subrat had remained silent and said the family had been unable to contact him since the murder.Police are now trying to establish whether Subrat knew about the alleged plan."Subrat has neither been arrested nor made an accused in the case," Commissioner of Police Raghubir Lal told PTI. He said his call detail records and other intelligence inputs were being examined."If his involvement is established during the investigation, action will be taken against him," Lal said.One of the questions investigators are trying to answer is how Shalu could allegedly communicate with Vishal while planning the murder without her husband becoming aware of it.According to police, Shalu arranged for Vishal and Raj Kishore to enter the apartment and hide in her bedroom before she left with Subrat for a party.The couple allegedly reached the lounge around 10.30pm and returned home around 3am, when they found Vineet's body.Investigators are now examining videos purportedly showing Shalu dancing at the gathering to establish whether they were recorded on the night of the murder."We are also examining communication between Shalu and Vishal. We have recovered data from their seized phones and are trying to retrieve deleted messages," Lal said.The investigation into their communication has thrown up what police describe as an extended exchange between Shalu and Vishal.A senior police official said Vishal had initially been sending Shalu good morning and good night messages without receiving a response. About three months before the murder, police said, she began replying and gradually started engaging with him.According to the officer, Shalu complimented Vishal on his appearance, telling him he was smart. She also asked whether he was in a relationship and why he had not yet married.Police believe the conversations marked the beginning of the alleged murder plan. Investigators suspect Shalu intentionally manipulated Vishal into carrying out the killing.The digital trail has become a key part of the investigation. Police said 49 messages exchanged between Shalu and Vishal from May 1 until the day of the murder had been deleted. During the same period, the two allegedly exchanged 309 calls.DCP West SM Qasim Abidi said Vishal deleted his chat history with Shalu after the murder, but was unable to completely erase the WhatsApp call records.Shalu's lawyer, Shivakant Dixit, has disputed the police characterisation of the gathering she attended on the night of the murder. articles.title: Pakistan stops Sikh pilgrims bound for Hemkund Sahib at Faisalabad airport
articles.summary: AMRITSAR: In a fresh setback to Pakistani Sikh pilgrims hoping to undertake the pilgrimage to Sri Hemkund Sahib in India, Pakistani authorities on Fri.
articles.body: AMRITSAR: In a fresh setback to Pakistani Sikh pilgrims hoping to undertake the pilgrimage to Sri Hemkund Sahib in India, Pakistani authorities on Friday prevented a jatha from travelling to India, leaving the devotees stranded at Faisalabad International Airport after they were asked to produce a No Objection Certificate (NOC), which the pilgrims claimed was not required for their journey.Jatha leader Papinder Singh informed in early Friday that the group was scheduled to fly from Faisalabad to Sharjah at 2.10am and then travel onwards to Delhi.However, immigration officials at the airport stopped them and sought an NOC before allowing them to board the flight.Papinder Singh said that, before the pilgrims reached the airport, Pakistan Punjab,s Sikh minority minister and president of the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (PSGPC), Ramesh Arora, along with Evacuee Trust Property Board deputy secretary Nasir Mushtaq, had met them at Nankana Sahib and allegedly pressured them not to travel to India by air and instead assured them to send via road through the Attari-Wagah land border.“The issue of the NOC was never raised with us before, but when immigration asked for NOC weasked Arora to provide them with NOC but he expressed his helplessness ",said he.The pilgrims, who were issued Indian visas covering Delhi, Amritsar, Sri Anandpur Sahib and Sri Hemkund Sahib, were waiting at Faisalabad airport for permission from the Pakistan government to travel to India.“We have already missed our Faisalabad-Sharjah flight and will also miss our onward flight from Sharjah to Delhi. Had we been allowed to travel as scheduled, we would have reached Delhi by Friday evening,” Singh said.The latest development comes amid continuing difficulties faced by Pakistani Sikh pilgrims following the closure of the Attari-Wagah land border.Singh said India had issued 92 visas to Sikh devotees seeking to visit Sri Hemkund Sahib, but the pilgrims had been forced to take a costly alternative air route by Pakistan government.They had spent nearly Pak Rs 2 crore on making all the arrangements and were now highly disappointed, praying to Waheguru at the airport, said the Jatha leader.He said they had appealed to the Pakistan government to grant special permission for the pilgrims to cross into India through the Attari-Wagah land route, arguing that this would save them from missing the pilgrimage to Sri Hemkund Sahib.“We are sitting at the airport, waiting for the Pakistan government to resolve the issue and allow us to proceed to India via the land route,” he added further.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Amritsar | Silver Rate in Amritsar | Bank Holidays in Amritsar | Public Holidays in Amritsar | Petrol Price in Amritsar | Diesel Price in Amritsar | CNG Price in Amritsar | LPG Price in AmritsarStay updated with the latest Amritsar news. articles.summary: Middle East News: More than 100 US military advisers are in Saudi Arabia helping the kingdom with intelligence and targeting as it battles Iran-backed Houthi forces in .
articles.body: More than 100 US military advisers are in Saudi Arabia helping the kingdom with intelligence and targeting as it battles Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen, five sources familiar with the operations told CNN.The US personnel are working under a joint forces command established in recent weeks, amid concerns that Iran is increasing its support for Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. One US official put the number of American troops involved at about 200.The deployment comes as fighting intensifies across the Arabian Peninsula and threatens to widen into a broader conflict. It also raises fears that another major shipping route out of the Middle East could be disrupted.US provides battlefield targeting supportThe US military has helped Saudi Arabia use a system that gives commanders a real-time view of battlefield developments, one US official told CNN. The official compared it with the Pentagon’s Maven system.Another source familiar with the cooperation said Washington was providing “geospatial” targeting support for Saudi strikes against the Houthis.The assistance is being provided as the Houthis expand their operations along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Military sources said the group seized the port city of Mocha on Thursday and moved towards strategic islands, including Hanish.Yemeni government military sources said the advances had given the Houthis greater leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern entrance to the Red Sea and one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.The Houthi-run humanitarian operations coordination centre said Red Sea navigation remained safe for all shipping companies except Saudi vessels. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam said the operations were defensive and would stop once attacks on Yemen ended.Shipping routes face fresh riskSaudi Arabia has relied more heavily on the Red Sea route since fighting involving Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.If the Houthis were able to restrict traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, Iran could gain a major strategic advantage by threatening a second key route for oil and other supplies. articles.title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
articles.summary: Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the 1989 crackdown.
articles.body:
Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.

Two of the defendants - Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 - were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law.

A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.

For years, Hong Kong was one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen Square crackdown - a topic that is highly sensitive and heavily censored in mainland China.

These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.

Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.

Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.

On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.

According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", according to a summary on Friday.

Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.

Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".

The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.

Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.

Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.

The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.

On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance.

"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks.

articles.title: How Iranian arms helped Houthis seize key Red Sea port in 'lightning' blitz
articles.summary: Middle East News: The Houthi takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Mocha was backed by a rapid offensive involving Iranian-supplied weapons, drones and direct guidan.
articles.body: The Houthi takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Mocha was backed by a rapid offensive involving Iranian-supplied weapons, drones and direct guidance from commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to Reuters. The attack came as Tehran seeks to open another pressure point against the United States and its ally Saudi Arabia.The lightning advance down Yemen’s western coast has given the Iran-backed group greater control over a strategically important stretch of the Red Sea, close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for global shipping, making the Houthi gains potentially significant for energy supplies and maritime trade.Reuters, citing Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources, reported that Iran instructed the Houthis last week to intensify attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised additional funding, weapons and senior officers to support the campaign. Several senior IRGC commanders had also travelled to Yemen to help oversee and command Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, according to a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran.Iranian weapons fuel Houthi blitzFive Saudi-backed Yemeni military sources told Reuters that the new Houthi campaign along the Tihama coastal plain began with a barrage of rocket fire and was directed by IRGC personnel. The sources, citing communications intercepts and accounts from captured Houthi fighters, said they believed the operation was being overseen by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a senior IRGC commander associated with the Qods Force.Iranian sources did not immediately confirm Shahlaei’s involvement. They said, however, that IRGC personnel had previously spent time in Yemen and that the force continued to move weapons and personnel into and out of Houthi-controlled areas despite an aerial and maritime blockade.The Houthis’ expanding arsenal appears to have played a key role in the speed of the offensive. Ahmed Nagi, a Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Reuters that the group’s military evolution had been driven by new weapons obtained either directly from Iran or through smuggling networks, particularly drones used in the latest offensive.Iran publicly denies directing the Houthis and says the group is an ally rather than a proxy. One Iranian official cited by Reuters said the move on Mocha was a Houthi decision, although it also served Tehran’s interests by putting upward pressure on oil prices and increasing pressure on the US and Saudi Arabia.Why Mocha matters to IranMocha is around 80 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow passage through which a significant share of global trade normally travels. The Houthis’ capture of the port therefore gives them a potentially stronger position to threaten shipping along one of the world’s key maritime routes.The development comes as traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb remains heavily disrupted by Houthi attacks. Shipping through the waterway has fallen sharply since the group began targeting vessels in late 2023, forcing many companies to divert around Africa.The strategic importance of the route has increased further as Iran’s conflict with the US and Israel has disrupted shipping through the nearby Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia had sought to reduce its dependence on Hormuz by routing oil through pipelines to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, but renewed Houthi threats have curtailed that activity, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence.The capture of Mocha also represents the Houthis’ biggest territorial gain since the 2022 truce that brought relative calm to Yemen after years of civil war. Its advance has raised fears that the country could slide back into a wider conflict, with the consequences potentially extending beyond Yemen to Saudi security, Red Sea shipping and global energy markets.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Princess Dianna's 'revenge dress' goes up for auction
articles.summary: Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to $300,000 (£220,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December.
articles.body:
A dress worn by Princess Diana to a party in London hours after a documentary was televised in which the then-Prince Charles admitted to committing adultery during their marriage is going up for auction.

Her dramatic arrival at the Serpentine Gallery in 1994 in a custom-made black silk evening dress by designer Christina Stambolian became an iconic pop-culture moment.

The media dubbed her outfit the "revenge dress".

Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to $300,000 (£220,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December.

A press release from Sotheby's said it is the first time the dress has been offered at auction since 1997, when the late princess sold 79 of her dresses to raise money for charities.

Morgane Halimi, Sotheby's Global Head of Handbags and Fashion, said in a statement that Princess Diana "understood instinctively" that fashion can be a language in its own right.

"On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life," Halimi said.

"She walked into a moment in which so much of her story was being told for her and, through what she chose to wear, reclaimed the narrative for herself."

According to Sotheby's, Anna Harvey, her stylist at the time, said Diana "wanted to look a million dollars".

The princess made a last-minute wardrobe change for the fundraising dinner and chose the strapless evening dress by the Greek designer Christina Stambolian - which she accessorised with a royal jewel, a black clutch and black pumps.

The vintage Jaguar XJ40 car that Diana arrived in at the event was sold at auction earlier this year for £66,250.

The revenge dress is expected to fetch a considerably higher price.

If it does, it will not be the first time an item from the princess's wardrobe has sold for a significant sum.

Princess Diana's sweater featuring a black sheep among rows of white ones was sold for £920,000 at an auction by Sotheby's in New York in 2023.

articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Thursday said his administration would not require congressional approval to implement his proposed \"Trump Dividend\", und.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Thursday said his administration would not require congressional approval to implement his proposed "Trump Dividend", under which every American citizen could receive $5,000 after the midterm elections.In an interview with CBS News, Trump called the proposed payments as "a great infusion" and said the money would have to be spent in the US rather than other countries."I think they will do it if we needed it. But we think not. The country is doing so well, we've taken in trillions of dollars in tariffs and other things. We have now over $20 trillion worth of manufacturing plants and other investments being made in the United States, which is far greater than ever before," Trump said."And we think it's something that'll be good. We do have one proviso, and that's that the money be spent... people spend their money in the United States. We don't want to have that money spent in other countries. We think it's something that's really good, popular and it's a great infusion," he added.Trump had earlier pledged during a keynote address at a convention in Dallas to pay every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress after the November midterm elections.Trump also used the interview, conducted at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, to urge his supporters to approach the midterm elections as if he were personally on the ballot."Now, this time I'm not running, so it's a big difference when you're running and not running," he said. "I'm just asking the people, all you people that are listening, pretend I'm running because we have to win."Trump said Republican victories were needed to preserve the country's current direction."This is very, very important," he said. "We can't let this, we have the hottest country anywhere in the world, and we can't let it go."The US Census Bureau estimates there are about 245 million US citizen adults. A banner at the event carried the message, “Raftaar nahi, sansakar” (Not speed, but values).Reacting to the video, Biocon founder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw praised the initiative. “I think India needs this kind of ‘schooling’ more than another driving lesson! Commendable move by the Daman Collector,” she said in a post on X.“Making Thar and Fortuner owners take an oath to drive safely, sometimes a little public pledge may work better than a thousand road signs!” she added.The Daman administration did not link the campaign to any specific accident or incident. articles.title: Maduro’s wife seeks house arrest, cites heart condition, weight loss
articles.summary: US News: Twenty-four-hour armed surveillance, recorded phone calls and video monitoring are among the conditions lawyers for Venezuela’s former first lady Cili.
articles.body: Twenty-four-hour armed surveillance, recorded phone calls and video monitoring are among the conditions lawyers for Venezuela’s former first lady Cilia Flores have proposed if she is allowed to await trial under home confinement. Visitors would also need approval from prosecutors and the court.Flores, 69, would remain within the Manhattan federal court district under the proposed arrangement. She and her husband, former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, 63, are scheduled to stand trial next June.Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez, who represent Flores, said in court papers filed on Wednesday that she “deserves the opportunity to await her trial while on home confinement”, Reuters reported.Lawyers cite worsening heart conditionFlores is being held at the Metropolitan Detention Centre in Brooklyn. Her lawyers say a longstanding heart condition has worsened while she has been in custody.Since her arrest, she has gone without an injection that her lawyers say she needs every month to manage mitral valve prolapse.Her treatment in custody includes baby aspirin, a statin and diltiazem, with nitroglycerine prescribed when needed for chest pain.The filing also says Flores has lost more than 11.3kg and two molars and continues to experience gastritis and reflux.Her lawyers said doctors have recommended cardiac catheterization, with further heart procedures possible afterwards. Donnelly and Sanchez said any such procedures would require adequate recovery time and a suitable setting.Flores, Maduro deny cocaine conspiracy chargesFlores and Maduro deny US charges accusing them of conspiring to send cocaine into the country and have entered not-guilty pleas.The couple are also seeking dismissal of the indictment. In a separate filing, they maintain that their positions as the leader and first lady of a foreign country give them immunity.An early-January US operation at their Caracas home ended with both being taken into custody. They were subsequently brought to New York.Lawyers acknowledge medical care in custodyDonnelly and Sanchez said jail staff had “been extremely respectful toward her and her husband” and that Flores “does not dispute that she has received excellent care from medical professionals” at the jail and hospital.They argued, however, that “a detention centre lacks the conditions needed for such a recovery”.Judge yet to rule on home-confinement requestFederal prosecutors have yet to respond to Flores’ application. The US attorney’s office in Manhattan declined to comment, while Judge Alvin K Hellerstein has not ruled on the request.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Prince William gets a 12-foot-6-inch crocodile named after him; it is the 300th animal in a decade-long climate study
articles.summary: UK News: Prince William has received an unusual new namesake, a 12-foot-6-inch saltwater crocodile living at Australia’s Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve. Conserva.
articles.body: Prince William has received an unusual new namesake, a 12-foot-6-inch saltwater crocodile living at Australia’s Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve. Conservationist Robert Irwin, son of the late wildlife expert Steve Irwin, gave the reptile the royal name after it became the 300th crocodile tagged through a long-running research project. The animal will now be monitored for the next decade, with researchers collecting information about its behaviour, diet and body temperature as they investigate how climate change could affect crocodiles and their ecosystem.Prince William now has a 12-foot-6-inch crocodile named after himThe enormous saltwater crocodile, measuring 3.8 metres or 12 feet 6 inches, was given its unusual name by Robert Irwin at the Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve in Queensland. Irwin chose the name in recognition of the Prince of Wales’s commitment to wildlife conservation. The crocodile is the 300th animal to be tagged as part of the reserve’s research programme. Irwin introduced the reptile as a “big boy” and “modern-day dinosaur”, turning a major scientific milestone into an unexpected tribute to a royal who has made environmental protection a central part of his public work.Robert Irwin linked the crocodile’s name to Prince William’s conservation workThe naming was not simply a playful reference to the future king. Robert Irwin explained the decision in comments reported by The Independent, saying the team wanted to recognise what he described as the “incredible conservation work” of His Royal Highness. Irwin also connected the moment with The Earthshot Prize, Prince William’s environmental initiative, which was launched as a 10-year programme to support solutions to some of the planet’s biggest environmental problems. Irwin serves as an ambassador for the prize and has developed a friendship with William through their shared interest in conservation.The 300th crocodile will be tracked for another 10 yearsThe royal namesake is also part of a serious scientific effort. The crocodile has been fitted with a small tracker and will be followed for the next 10 years. According to The Independent, researchers hope the monitoring will reveal what the animal eats, how long it can remain underwater and how changes in climate affect its body temperature. The BBC likewise highlighted the crocodile as the 300th animal involved in the decade-long study. Rather than simply observing individual animals, the long-term project is designed to build a much larger picture of crocodile ecology and environmental change.The study could show how climate change affects crocodilesTemperature is particularly significant for crocodiles because they are ectothermic animals, meaning their body temperature is strongly influenced by their surroundings. Long-term tracking of tagged animals can therefore provide researchers with information about how individual crocodiles respond to changing environmental conditions. The 300th crocodile represents another data point in a study that has been running for years at the Steve Irwin Wildlife Reserve. The latest animal will provide information over the coming decade, allowing researchers to examine behaviour and physiology while also gathering evidence relevant to the conservation of the species and its wider ecosystem.The unusual tribute brings together two very different kinds of public figures through a shared interest in conservation. Prince William has made environmental action a major part of his work through The Earthshot Prize, while Robert Irwin continues the wildlife legacy of his father, Steve Irwin. Now, a 12-foot-6-inch saltwater crocodile carries the prince’s name, while simultaneously becoming part of a long-term scientific record that could help researchers understand how crocodiles respond to a changing climate.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ED raids Ramnandi Hotels in alleged Rs 132-crore bank fraud case; 9 locations searched
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Friday conducted searches at nine locations in Bihar, Haryana and Delhi in connection with an alleged b.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Friday conducted searches at nine locations in Bihar, Haryana and Delhi in connection with an alleged bank fraud involving Ramnandi Hotels and Resorts Ltd (RHRL), Gaya. The searches were carried out under Section 17 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) at six locations in Gaya, two in Gurugram and one in New Delhi, officials said.RHRL is controlled by Akhouri Gopal and his sons, Nishant and Nitesh, according to officials. The ED action follows an investigation into the alleged diversion of loan funds and suspected attempts to move properties to prevent possible attachment.During the probe, the agency found that RHRL allegedly diverted Rs 58 crore out of the Rs 85 crore disbursed by a consortium of banks led by Central Bank of India. The loans were allegedly obtained on the basis of fake or forged project completion reports provided by the company's chartered accountant.The loan facilities were also backed by personal guarantees from Akhouri Gopal and his family members, officials said.The investigation has also flagged five properties that had been pledged or mortgaged with Tata Motors Ltd against outstanding dues of a related group entity. The properties were allegedly sold recently despite being pledged.According to the ED, the properties were sold at grossly undervalued prices, with the sale deeds showing the consideration as cash receipts. Some of the buyers are suspected to be benamis or proxies of Akhouri Gopal, officials said.The agency suspects the transactions were aimed at alienating the properties and preventing coercive action. Some of the buyers were reportedly people of modest means who may not have had the financial capacity to arrange the amounts involved in the transactions.The proceeds of crime in the case, based on the CBI chargesheet, are estimated at around Rs 131.79 crore, corresponding to the non-performing asset (NPA) value, officials said.The searches are part of the ED's ongoing investigation into the alleged bank fraud and related movement of assets.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Philippine rescuers board burning ferry 40 hours after blaze began
articles.summary: Thick, toxic fumes and extreme temperatures pose a challenge to rescuers who have boarded the ship.
articles.body:
More than 40 hours after a deadly ferry fire began, Philippine rescuers have boarded the MV June Aster in search of dozens of missing people.

Five people have been killed while 43 people have been rescued, many of whom are receiving treatment in hospital. Eighty-four people remain missing.

Photos shared by the coastguard on Friday morning show smoke still curling from the ferry, which was on its way from the capital Manila to the island of Coron.

Officials have struggled to board the hull since search and rescue operations began on Wednesday of the toxic fumes and heat. They finally got on at about 11:30 on Friday, the coastguard say.

"The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab had earlier told the BBC.

"No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier.

Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide.

Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 – two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say.

Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses.

The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab says.

Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.

A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening.

Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat.

"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC.

He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.

"It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said.

The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire.

The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.

Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.

"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.
